plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 9: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
plan.contextChunk: This figure is one graph on a dotted coordinate grid showing two straight lines and the point at which they cross. The horizontal axis is labeled x and carries integer ticks from -6 to 6; the vertical axis is labeled y with integer ticks from -5 to 5, and each axis ends in arrowheads. A blue line of negative slope enters at the upper left and descends to the lower right, meeting the vertical axis just below the origin; a blue label at the left edge reads x + 2y = -1. A red line of positive slope climbs from the lower left to the upper right and meets the vertical axis at 3; a red label at the lower left reads -x + y = 3. Both lines end in arrowheads at each extremity. A filled black dot marks the single crossing, in the second quadrant just left of the vertical axis and slightly above the horizontal axis, and the coordinates printed above it read (-7/3, 2/3) with the fractions stacked. Drawing both equations against shared axes converts the algebraic system into a picture whose solution is a location. The graph makes visible that these lines meet at exactly one point, so the system has a single solution.

interactionPlan.concept: The solution of a system of two linear equations is the point where their lines cross — the single ordered pair that satisfies both equations — and changing either line's equation moves, eliminates, or preserves that crossing.
elements: x-axis labeled 'x' with integer ticks -6 to 6 and arrowheads at both ends
y-axis labeled 'y' with integer ticks -5 to 5 and arrowheads at both ends
dotted grid covering the plotting area
blue line of negative slope, labeled 'x + 2y = -1' in blue at the left edge, arrowheads at both ends
red line of positive slope, labeled '-x + y = 3' in red at the lower left, arrowheads at both ends
filled black dot marking the intersection point
stacked-fraction coordinate label '(-7/3, 2/3)' above the black dot
readout panel showing both equations with the dot's coordinates substituted and verified

interactions.label: Blue line: x + 2y = c (choose c)
interactions.teaches: Shifting the blue line's intercept slides the whole line parallel to itself and drags the intersection point along the red line — the solution is wherever the two equations are simultaneously true, and it can leave the visible grid without ceasing to exist

interactions.label: Red line slope m in y = mx + 3
interactions.teaches: Rotating the red line about its y-intercept moves the crossing continuously, and when its slope matches the blue line's (-1/2) the lines become parallel and the system has no solution
Clicking the intersection dot substitutes its coordinates into both equations at once, showing that the solution is the one ordered pair that makes both equations true simultaneously

demo_steps.title: The solution as a point
demo_steps.narration: The blue line x + 2y = -1 and the red line -x + y = 3 cross at exactly one point, (-7/3, 2/3). That single point is the system's solution — the only (x, y) pair lying on both lines.

demo_steps.title: Shift the blue line
demo_steps.narration: Drag the intercept slider: the blue line slides parallel to itself and the intersection point travels along the red line. Every value of c gives a different system with a different single solution — until the crossing leaves the grid, though it still exists.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the red line
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slope slider: the red line pivots about its y-intercept of 3 and the crossing moves continuously. Near m = -1/2 the crossing races off to infinity — the lines turn parallel and the system has no solution at all.

demo_steps.title: Verify by substitution
demo_steps.narration: Return to the original lines and click the black dot: its coordinates are substituted into both equations, and each side balances. The intersection is the solution precisely because the same pair satisfies both equations.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A system's solution is a location: the point where both lines cross, because that is the only ordered pair making both equations true at once — and if the lines are parallel, no such location exists.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Dotted light-gray grid on white, bold black axes with arrowheads, axis labels x (right) and y (top) in italic. Blue line y = -(x+1)/2 crossing the y-axis at -0.5, red line y = x + 3 crossing at y = 3; both with arrowheads on their ends. Equation labels placed in their line's color at the left/lower-left margins as in the original. Intersection dot at (-7/3, 2/3) — second quadrant, just left of the y-axis — with its stacked-fraction label directly above. When sliders move lines, the dot and its coordinate readout update live; when the lines are parallel, show a 'no solution — parallel lines' note where the dot was. The click-activated substitution readout shows each equation with x and y replaced by the dot's current coordinates and a checkmark when both sides are equal.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for the blue line's y-intercept: the learner shifts x + 2y = c up or down, the intersection point with the red line moves or exits the grid, and a system's solution is seen as the point satisfying both equations.
- Slider for the red line's slope: the learner rotates -x + y = 3 about its y-intercept, the crossing location updates and can become parallel to the blue line, clarifying how line orientation controls whether there is one or no visible solution.
- Click on the intersection point: the learner selects the black dot, both equations highlight and substitute the dot's coordinates, showing that the same ordered pair makes both equations true.

authoredContext:
We gain an important perspective on systems of equations by looking at the graphical representation. See the figure to find that the equations intersect at the solution. We do not need to ask whether there may be a second solution because observing the graph confirms that the system has exactly one solution.

This graph displays a system of two linear equations plotted on a coordinate plane. The blue line represents the equation x + 2y = -1, while the red line represents the equation -x + y = 3. The point where these two lines intersect, indicated by a black dot, is the solution to the system of equations and is labeled as (-7/3, 2/3). The x-axis ranges from -6 to 6, and the y-axis ranges from -5 to 5, with a grid background to aid in reading the coordinates.

discrepancies: the side-panel readout and verification popup give the solution as rounded decimals '(-2.33, 0.67)' while the source figure presents the exact fractional coordinates (−7/3, 2/3)

the on-canvas coordinate label sits directly above the intersection dot and overlaps the red line (masked by a white backing box), whereas the source tucks it cleanly between the two lines to the upper right of the dot
when the red slope slider moves off m = 1, the red equation label rewrites itself as 'y = mx + 3' rather than keeping the source's '-x + y = 3' standard form
evaluation.notes: A faithful reproduction of the two-line system with correct slopes, arrowheaded axes and lines, dotted grid, and exact intersection, enriched by functional sliders, a four-step guided demo, and a working substitution-verification interaction; only the decimal (rather than fractional) readout and a slight label/line overlap deviate from the source.
action_items: Use the existing toFrac() helper in renderReadout() and the verification popup so the solution and substituted values display as exact fractions (−7/3, 2/3) matching the source, not rounded decimals.
Offset the coordinate label to the upper right of the dot, between the two lines as in the source, so it no longer overlaps the red line even with its white backing box.
